answer.rationale: The finance mandate for 18% component spend reduction and the low-cost vendor's quote that meets this target alone create a forcing function. memory_c2 documents that the low-cost vendor delivered sharp unit cost cuts with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing—this is the most directly relevant prior evidence. memory_c4 shows renegotiation is possible at renewal, but with 14 days remaining and no auto-renewal clause, relying on negotiation leaves execution risk. memory_c6 shows multi-year commitments unlock volume pricing with the incumbent, but the incumbent cannot deliver the 18% cut alone. The assembly line at 94% capacity creates real delivery risk, so switching requires verification that the low-cost vendor can sustain current SLA. However, deferring past quarter-end (memory_c5 precedent) is not available—the contract expires and does not auto-renew. A second source (memory_c3 precedent) would preserve buffer but does not address the cost mandate. Switching to the low-cost vendor is the only path that satisfies both cost and timeline constraints; the onboarding speed documented in memory_c2 and their track record on invoicing accuracy reduce execution risk relative to the tight 14-day window.
